summary: A 1970 note giving BBN's comments on the host-host protocol proposed in RFC 33, which it updates. BBN was the company building the network's message processors.

eli5.summary: The company building the network's boxes sent in its feedback on a proposed set of rules.

questions: why imp buffers must be empty
subtitle: BBN's engineer explains why an IMP's buffers must stay empty, and why hosts should do the buffering.

tldr.problem: The host protocol paper in RFC 33 assumed the network could hold messages for long periods and that the IMP could buffer several for a host to pick from.
tldr.mechanism: Bill Crowther of BBN argues that IMP buffering is minimal, exists to absorb traffic surges, and is useless unless the buffers are empty.
tldr.outcome: He concludes that buffering for users is a host function and should stay in the hosts, and he names the sentences in RFC 33 he disputes.

today: RFC 47 updates RFC 33 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an early design discussion rather than a specification, and its status is listed as Unknown.

sections.title: Why This Note Exists
sections.content:
Jon Postel and Steve Crocker of UCLA introduce the note. BBN had sent comments on RFC 33 but did not want to publish them for fear of embarrassing the authors. UCLA found them useful and shared them anyway. The author is Bill Crowther.

He calls the host protocol paper otherwise excellent, but finds two substantial errors, both rooted in a misunderstanding of the IMP as a communications device.
sections.eli5: A helpful letter from the box builders was shared with everybody, because it was too useful to keep private.

sections.title: The IMP Is Not a Waiting Room
sections.content:
The criticised paper treated the network as something you push a message into, which then waits in buffers for a long time. The author says a better model is that the message pops out an instant after it is inserted. The delay that exists comes mostly from phone line hardware.

IMP buffering is minimal and is devoted to error control and momentary traffic surges. Because the IMP cannot force a Host to take a message, BBN built an elaborate RFNM mechanism that suspends new input until the Host does. The aim is that as the Host takes one message the next arrives on the phone line, with no buffering at all.

That cannot be fully achieved, so buffers exist for surges. They only help when empty: the IMP's buffers must be empty or they are not serving their communication purpose.
sections.eli5: Think of a pipe, not a bucket. The box passes messages through right away, and its little catch-basin is only for sudden splashes, so it has to be empty.

sections.title: The Two Errors
sections.content:
The first error is on page 5 of the paper, which assumed a user does not use multiple links to get a wide band. The author replies that achieving wider band is a primary purpose of links. BBN's trouble comes from an imbalance of input and output, not wide band. The paper did notice that multiple links subvert the RFNM mechanism, but it mislabeled the problem.

Page 5 also assumed the network's load comes from users sending sequences of messages rather than many users sending single messages. The author says random single messages are easy because the statistics favour BBN. The problems come from non-random coincidences, so BBN takes special precautions against bursts.

The second error is on pages 23 and 24, where four sentences imply the design could improve if the Host could choose which of several waiting inputs to accept. The author violently disagrees that the IMP can do that buffering.
sections.eli5: Two ideas in the paper were wrong. Sending lots of messages at once is fine; what hurts is when too much arrives and too little leaves.

sections.title: Why Hosts Should Buffer
sections.content:
In ideal operation there would be at most one message waiting for the Host. With more than one, the IMP urgently needs the Host to accept them, because its ability to handle surges falls below standard. At the time, an IMP allowed three full length messages for its Host before backing traffic up in the network, which the author says is not enough both to help the Host and to keep a reserve.

To the question of why not simply add memory to the IMP, the answer is that buffering is a Host function, differs in each time share system, is hard to control over a busy serial channel, might not be needed in some places, and is better done where the memory can be shared by the Host operating system.

The note closes by listing the disputed sentences by paragraph and sentence number, noting that one sentence mentions 80ms being hardware screw adjustable.
sections.eli5: Keeping a line of waiting messages is the host computer's job, because it knows its own needs and has memory it can share.

references.text: NWG/RFC 33, the Host Protocol paper that BBN comments on.
